title: Numbers With Balanced Digit Halves
statement:
Call a positive integer balanced if it has an even number of digits, 2k, and the sum of its first k digits equals the sum of its last k digits. For example, 2413 is balanced because 2 + 4 = 1 + 3.

Numbers with an odd number of digits are never balanced.

Given low and high, return how many balanced numbers lie in the range [low, high], both ends included.

examples.why: The two-digit balanced numbers are 11, 22, …, 99. 100 has three digits.
The first half sums to 3, so the last two digits must also sum to 3: 1203, 1212, 1221 and 1230.
Every number here has three digits, an odd count, so none can be balanced, not even 111.

hints: The range is small enough to test every number one by one. The work is in the test itself.
Turn the number into its digits, check the count is even, then compare the sums of the two halves.
Below 10 001 only 2-digit and 4-digit numbers can qualify. For a 2-digit number that means the digits are equal; for a 4-digit number compare a + b with c + d using / and %.

explain.intuition:
With at most 10 000 numbers to check, testing each one directly is the intended solution. For each number, split it into digits. If the digit count is odd, skip it. Otherwise add up the left half and the right half and compare.

The bound also tells you that only 2-digit and 4-digit numbers matter. A 2-digit number is balanced exactly when x % 11 === 0. A 4-digit number abcd is balanced when ⌊x/1000⌋ + ⌊x/100⌋ % 10 === ⌊x/10⌋ % 10 + x % 10. That avoids building strings, but the plain string version is just as correct.
steps: Write x as a digit string s. If its length is odd, skip it.
Sum the first half and the second half of the digits.
If the sums are equal, count x. Return the count.
pitfalls: Treating odd-length numbers like 121 or 111 as balanced by comparing around the middle digit. The rule needs an even length.
Excluding high, or starting at low + 1. Both ends are part of the range.
Comparing the digit sequences instead of their sums. 1230 is balanced although 12 and 30 differ.

complexity.time: O((high − low) · d), d = number of digits

solutions.title: Check each number through its digit string
solutions.idea: Convert to a string, require an even length, and compare the sums of the two halves.

solutions.title: Arithmetic on 2-digit and 4-digit numbers
solutions.idea: Under the bound, only 2-digit and 4-digit numbers can qualify. Read their digits with division and remainder.

followups: Answer many (low, high) queries quickly. What would you precompute?
Now high can be 10¹⁸. How would a digit DP count balanced numbers without listing them?
